note.text: Simple present can describe a habit or general situation; simple past can present an event as completed in the past. Present progressive uses a present form of be with -ing, while present perfect uses have or has with a past participle. Time reference depends on context, not the form alone. A participle is not automatically a finite verb group. Choose auxiliaries and agreement as well as the lexical form. The exercises name the required pattern so that a different valid meaning is not unfairly marked as the same target.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to form simple, progressive and perfect groups and explain why a complete auxiliary pattern matters. Builds on: word functions, spelling and study language. Leads to: clause structure, sequence of tenses and conditional meanings.

sections.heading: Read the original model
sections.text: Original models: Bih {thirdPerson("write")} the club summary as a regular duty. Yesterday she {past("write")} it. At this moment she is {ing("write")} it. She has {participle("write")} the current summary. The changing groups present different viewpoints; the form written alone does not supply every complete clause.

sections.heading: Apply and check
sections.text: Find the subject and the requested pattern, then assemble the full group. Check the distinction between past and participle for irregular verbs. In your own writing, choose the form that fits the intended situation rather than changing tenses without a reason.
